slides.title: What Is Governance?
slides.kicker: Not just orders — a team effort!
bullets: Governance is the process where institutions and citizens work together to decide, act, and stay answerable.
Democratic governance rests on four foundations: transparency, accountability, participation, and the rule of law.
It places citizens at the centre of the political process, making it people-centric and welfare-oriented.
slides.note: Governance = government plus people, in action!

slides.title: A Town in Heavy Rain
slides.kicker: Floods hit — who saves the day?
bullets: Days of unusually heavy rainfall flood roads, close schools, disrupt electricity, and raise public health concerns.
People struggle to reach schools, workplaces, and even hospitals across the town.
During such situations, organisations and individuals come together to help all in need.

items: Daily life comes to a halt

slides.note: Think of your own town during monsoon.

slides.title: Many Hands, Many Roles
slides.kicker: One crisis, many kinds of helpers
bullets: The municipal corporation clears drains and removes garbage; the Public Works Department repairs damaged roads.
The police manage traffic while school authorities inform parents that schools will remain closed.
Health workers prevent disease, local representatives raise concerns, and residents volunteer and report flooded areas.
slides.note: Count the helpers — more than six!

slides.title: Why Together Wins
slides.kicker: Alone we struggle, together we fix
bullets: No single department can solve a flood-like crisis on its own because roads, health, traffic, and schools are all affected.
If departments did not communicate or coordinate with one another, the response would break down.
Solving public problems needs much more than a government issuing orders.
slides.note: Coordination is the secret ingredient.

slides.title: Government vs Governance
bullets: Government refers to the institutions and authorities that exercise political power.
Governance is the process by which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored in the public interest.
The two terms are closely related, but they are not synonymous.

right.title: Governance
items: Government, citizens, media, civil society, private organisations
Focuses on how governing is carried out

slides.note: Who governs vs how governing happens.

slides.title: The Full Governance Team
bullets: Government includes the Legislature, the Executive, and the Judiciary.
Governance includes government, citizens, media, civil society, and private organisations.
Good governance makes policies transparent, accountable, effective, and responsive to people's needs.
slides.note: Media and civil society join the game too.

slides.title: The Street Light Test
bullets: Installing street lights is government work: the municipal corporation or panchayat holds the authority to provide this public service.
Planning, maintaining, and improving the lights is governance: people identify dark spots, report non-functional lights, and give feedback.
Governance ensures continuous delivery of public services like well-lit streets and greater public safety.
slides.note: Spot more such examples in your daily life.

slides.title: Governance Is Everywhere
bullets: Governance is the way a country, state, city, village, school, or organisation is managed.
It is the system through which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored for the welfare of the people.
Understanding governance is essential to know how government impacts our lives.
slides.note: Even your school has governance!

slides.title: Institutions and Function
slides.kicker: Structure shapes how work gets done
bullets: Government is the institutional aspect, while governance is its functional aspect.
The government's institutional setup influences the nature of governance.
Governance initiatives in turn require institutional adaptations to implement policies and schemes.
slides.note: Two sides of one coin.

slides.title: Life Before Colonial Rule
bullets: European powers colonised many societies, particularly in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
Before colonial rulers forced their own models, these societies governed themselves through local and organic systems.
Most colonies became independent by the end of the 20th century, yet colonial institutions largely persisted.

left.title: Before colonial rule
items: Own models of governance and policy-making

slides.note: Remember colonialism from Grade 8?

slides.title: India's Two Special Ways
bullets: India preserved most of its knowledge of pre-colonial institutions and governance traditions through texts and practices.
After Independence in 1947, replacing all colonial institutions at once was not possible.
India's leaders framed the Constitution in the spirit of India's own values and ideals.
slides.note: Old wisdom, modern democracy.

slides.title: Mottos Tell the Story
bullets: The British Order of the Star of India had the motto 'Heaven's Light, Our Guide'; India adopted 'Satyamev Jayate' after Independence.
The Supreme Court chose 'Yato Dharmastato Jayah' from the Mahabharata, meaning 'Where there is Dharma, there is victory'.
These changes are not merely symbolic; they signify core values and ideals.

left.title: British era
items: Order of the Star of India

right.title: After Independence
items: Satyamev Jayate, from the Mundaka Upanishad
Yato Dharmastato Jayah, from the Mahabharata

slides.note: Truth alone triumphs!

slides.title: The Sengol Story
slides.kicker: A thousand-year mark of righteous rule
bullets: The Sengol, a cultural marker of rulership and good governance, was placed in the new Parliament building in 2023 by PM Narendra Modi.
The tradition began more than a thousand years ago during the reign of the Chola dynasty.
At midnight on 15th August 1947, Jawaharlal Nehru received the Sengol from the Adheenam Saints of Tamil Nadu.
slides.note: An old Shaivite tradition lives on.

slides.title: Ram Rajya and Rajadharma
bullets: Gandhi visualised ideal governance as Ram Rajya, rooted in probity, transparency, compassion, welfare, and people-centric spirit.
From the Vedic period to the Ramayana and Mahabharata, governance was seen as a sacred responsibility, not just a means of power.
Rajadharma, the foremost duty of an ideal king, was to protect the people by upholding Dharma and promote the welfare of society.
slides.note: Ram Rajya shines in the Ramayana and Ramcharitamanas.

slides.title: Wisdom of the Ancients
bullets: Kautilya's Arthashastra says: Prajasukhe sukham rajnah prajanam cha hite hitam.
It means in the happiness of the people lies the happiness of the ruler, and in the interest of the people lies the interest of the ruler.
The Rigveda refers to the Sabha and Samiti as institutions where matters of governance and public welfare were discussed.
slides.note: Good governance was measured by peace, prosperity, justice, and well-being.

slides.title: Good Governance Daily
slides.kicker: What good governance does for you
bullets: It maintains law and order so that people can live safely and peacefully.
It protects the rights and freedom of citizens, which are essential in a democratic society.
It helps people access public services such as education, healthcare, and transport, and promotes justice and fairness.
slides.note: Governance touches your whole day.

slides.title: Governance Never Finishes
bullets: The task of governance is always ongoing.
With time, the needs, desires, and aspirations of people evolve, creating new challenges.
The government and its institutions have to keep responding to these changing demands.
slides.note: Governance is a journey, not a destination.

slides.title: Four Big Challenges
slides.kicker: Know the obstacles to fix them
bullets: Weak coordination between institutions and departments can affect the implementation of government programmes.
Unequal access to public services can leave behind groups facing social, economic, or geographical barriers.
Malpractices and misuse of public offices stop resources and benefits from reaching the people.
Misinformation and fake news also pose a serious challenge to good governance.
slides.note: Fake news is a governance problem too.

slides.title: Who Fixes the Challenges
bullets: Addressing these challenges requires effective institutions and responsible officials.
It also needs active citizens and a continued commitment to the principles of good governance.
Shared responsibility keeps democratic governance healthy.
slides.note: You are part of the answer.

slides.title: E-Governance Steps In
slides.kicker: A big helper for good governance
bullets: The initiative of e-governance has contributed significantly towards good governance.
Details about e-governance are explored in the section that follows this one.
25th December is celebrated as National Good Governance Day.
slides.note: Ask why 25th December was chosen!

quiz.q: In the book's flood example, which department repaired the damaged roads?
quiz.why: The Public Works Department repairs damaged roads while other bodies handle drains, traffic, and health.

quiz.q: Democratic governance is based on transparency, accountability, participation, and which other principle?
quiz.why: The four foundations are transparency, accountability, participation, and the rule of law.

quiz.q: Why could no single department solve the flood crisis alone?
options: Each department had too little staff
The crisis affected roads, health, traffic, and schools together
Departments are not allowed to act in emergencies
Only citizens were affected, not departments
quiz.why: Flooding disrupted many services at once, and the situation improved with the collective efforts of all.

quiz.q: Which question does government focus on, compared to governance?
quiz.why: Government focuses on who governs; governance focuses on how governing is carried out.

quiz.q: In the street light example, identifying dark spots and reporting non-functional lights shows which side?
options: Government, because the corporation owns the lights
Governance, because citizens join the process of delivery
Private organisations, because they build roads
quiz.why: Governance is the ongoing process involving people in planning, reporting, and feedback.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the book's distinction between government and governance?
options: Government makes decisions while governance only announces them
Government is the institutions with political authority while governance is the process of decision-making and implementation
Government and governance are exactly synonymous
Governance includes only elected leaders while government includes everyone
quiz.why: Government is institutional; governance is the functional process including citizens, media, and civil society.

quiz.q: From which text is the national motto 'Satyamev Jayate' taken?
quiz.why: Satyamev Jayate, meaning Truth alone triumphs, comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly lists the two ways India stands out from other colonised societies?
options: It forgot its traditions and copied colonial models
It kept pre-colonial knowledge and framed its Constitution on its own values
It replaced all institutions at once in 1947
quiz.why: India preserved its governance traditions through texts and practices and framed the Constitution in the spirit of its own ideals.

quiz.q: According to the book, what do motto changes like adopting Satyamev Jayate actually signify?
options: Only a decorative change of words
Core values and ideals, not merely symbolic changes
A complete break from Indian tradition
A plan to restore colonial institutions
quiz.why: The changes signify core values and ideals, reflecting the continuing importance of Indian ethical values in public life.

quiz.q: In which year was the Sengol placed in the newly inaugurated Parliament building?
quiz.why: Prime Minister Narendra Modi placed the Sengol in the new Parliament building in 2023.

quiz.q: According to Kautilya's Arthashastra, where does the ruler's happiness lie?
options: In the happiness of the people
In the size of the treasury
In the strength of the army
quiz.why: Prajasukhe sukham rajnah: in the happiness of the people lies the happiness of the ruler.

quiz.q: How was good governance measured in Indian tradition, beyond the ruler's authority?
options: By the number of forts a king built
By peace, prosperity, justice, and well-being in society
By the taxes collected each year
By the victories in battles alone
quiz.why: Good governance was measured by the peace, prosperity, justice, and well-being in society.

quiz.q: On which date is National Good Governance Day celebrated?
quiz.why: 25th December is celebrated as National Good Governance Day.

quiz.q: Which modern problem does the book list as a serious challenge to good governance?
quiz.why: Misinformation and fake news pose a serious challenge to good governance.

quiz.q: What combination does the book say is needed to address governance challenges?
options: Effective institutions, responsible officials, active citizens, and continued commitment
quiz.why: Addressing challenges requires effective institutions, responsible officials, active citizens, and commitment to good governance principles.

examples.title: The Flooded Town Response Map
examples.problem: Your town experiences several days of unusually heavy rainfall. Roads flood, schools close, electricity is disrupted, and public health concerns rise. Using the book's example, list which organisations and individuals act, what each one does, and why the response succeeds.
steps: Identify the crisis: flooded roads, closed schools, disrupted electricity, and rising public health concerns.
Match civic bodies to roles: the municipal corporation clears drains and removes garbage; the Public Works Department repairs damaged roads.
Add safety and information roles: the police manage traffic; school authorities inform parents that schools will remain closed; health workers prevent the spread of diseases.
Add people's roles: local representatives raise people's concerns; residents volunteer to help vulnerable neighbours and report on flooded areas.
Conclude: the situation improves with the collective efforts of all, because institutions communicate, coordinate, and remain accountable.
examples.answer: The crisis is handled through governance: different institutions and citizens working together, making decisions, implementing them, and remaining accountable.

examples.title: Sorting Government from Governance
examples.problem: Your colony has several dark spots at night because street lights are not working. Following the book's street light example, separate the government's part from the governance part in solving this problem.
steps: Spot the authority: the municipal corporation or panchayat has the authority to provide the public service of street lighting. That is government.
Spot the process: planning the lighting, implementing it, and maintaining it is governance.
Include the people: residents identify dark spots, report non-functional lights, and provide feedback.
Check the outcome: continuous delivery of the public service, giving well-lit streets and greater public safety.
examples.answer: Government installs the lights as the authority; governance keeps them working through a continuous process that involves people at every step.

examples.title: Tracing Values Through Mottos
examples.problem: Independent India changed the mottos it inherited. Trace each motto to its source and explain what the change signifies.
steps: Note the old motto: the British 'Order of the Star of India' used 'Heaven's Light, Our Guide'.
Note the new motto: after Independence, India adopted 'Satyamev Jayate' (Truth alone triumphs) from the Mundaka Upanishad as its national motto.
Add the judiciary: the Supreme Court of India chose 'Yato Dharmastato Jayah' from the Mahabharata, meaning 'Where there is Dharma, there is victory'.
Explain the significance: these changes are not merely symbolic; they signify core values and ideals, reflecting the continuing importance of Indian ethical values in public life.
examples.answer: The new mottos show India drawing on traditional ideas and values of governance and adapting them to the needs of a modern democracy.

flowchart.title: How governance responds to a public problem

steps.label: Public problem appears
steps.detail: Heavy rain floods roads, closes schools, and disrupts electricity.

steps.label: Actors come together
steps.detail: Departments, local representatives, and residents coordinate instead of acting alone.

steps.label: Decisions are made
steps.detail: Choices are made in the public interest, keeping citizens at the centre.

steps.label: Work is implemented
steps.detail: Drains are cleared, roads repaired, traffic managed, and health risks controlled.

steps.label: Citizens participate
steps.detail: People volunteer, report flooded areas, and give feedback.

steps.label: Accountability is maintained
steps.detail: Actions are monitored so delivery stays transparent and responsive.

steps.label: New challenges emerge
steps.detail: Weak coordination, unequal access, malpractice, and misinformation test the system.

steps.label: E-governance strengthens response
steps.detail: E-governance contributes significantly towards good governance.
